openers.late-pleistocene-age: The Late Pleistocene opened in warmth. The Last Interglacial followed the Penultimate Glacial Period, and an exceptionally intense humid period greened northern Africa, more strongly than its later Holocene counterpart. Hippos waded as far north as northern England, and sea level probably stood 6 to 9 m above today's. Modern humans were on the move, leaving stone tools in Arabia at least 125,000 years ago and fossils in Israel's caves, while in Java the last Homo erectus lived beside the Solo River. This chapter follows that warm start into the long Last Glacial Period, and the people and animals that lived through it.

late-001.title: A green Sahara opens a road out of Africa
late-001.text: The Sahara was not always a barrier. During the Last Interglacial, an exceptionally intense humid period greened northern Africa, more strongly than its later Holocene counterpart. Lakes and grasslands opened pathways for early humans across northern Africa and Arabia. Modern humans dispersed through North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula at least between 130,000 and 115,000 years ago. Timing mattered. The Red Sea coastal route was extremely dry before 140,000 and after 115,000 years ago. Such humid phases come with interglacials and with precession minima, points in the slow wobble of Earth's axis, while glacial stages bring dry spells.

late-002.title: The Eemian, the Last Interglacial
late-002.text: Around 125,000 years ago, forests grew at North Cape, Norway, where today there is only tundra. This was the Last Interglacial, also called the Eemian, or Marine Isotope Stage 5e. It followed the Penultimate Glacial Period and lasted until about 115,000 years ago. It was one of the warmest spells of the last 800,000 years, up to about 2 °C warmer than the Holocene, with carbon dioxide near 280 ppm. Warmth peaked about 128,000 to 123,000 years ago. Arctic summers ran about 2 to 4 °C warmer than in 2011. The warmth was not steady. Abrupt cold spells around 120,000 years ago followed shifts in the North Atlantic Current, the ocean stream that carries tropical heat north. The start of this interglacial, at the end of the Riss glaciation, is the proposed beginning of the Late Pleistocene.

late-003.title: Hippos wallow in northern England
late-003.text: Hippos once wallowed near Stockton-on-Tees in northern England. Interglacial warmth let them range that far north, though outside southern Europe they rarely went east of the Rhine. Europe's temperate landscapes also held straight-tusked elephants, Merck's and narrow-nosed rhinos, Irish elk, aurochs, cave lions and cave hyenas. Warmer seas let tropical 'Senegalese' marine snails, such as cone shells, colonize the Mediterranean.

late-004.title: Seas rise as West Antarctic ice collapses
late-004.text: The last time Earth was about as warm as the early 21st century, the West Antarctic Ice Sheet appears to have collapsed. That was around 125,000 years ago. At its peak, sea level stood probably 6 to 9 m above today's. Greenland's melting, the expansion of warming seawater and Antarctica all contributed. East Antarctica's Wilkes Basin alone lost ice worth about 0.5 m. Seas may have risen as fast as 2.5 m per century. The high water made islands of Fennoscandia and Jutland and flooded much of northwestern Europe and the West Siberian Plain. Fossil coral reefs from that highstand are now stranded above the sea, common in the Caribbean and along the Red Sea.

late-005.title: Klasies River: life on the South African coast
late-005.text: Caves on South Africa's coast held early people with a varied menu. Excavations at Klasies River found Middle Stone Age homes beginning about 125,000 years ago. Close to both shore and grassland, the people exploited marine life and land animals alike. Their remains include jaws about 119,000 years old and finger bones 90,000 to 100,000 years old.

late-006.title: Modern humans reach Arabia
late-006.text: Stone tools at Jebel Faya, in the United Arab Emirates, show modern humans in Arabia at least 125,000 years ago. Groups may have left Africa by two routes. One ran along the Nile, through Sinai and into the Levant. The other crossed the Bab-el-Mandeb strait when seas were low. On a raised reef 125,000 years old at Abdur, Eritrea, tools suggest coastal foragers ate shellfish over 100,000 years ago. These early ventures do not seem to have led to lasting settlement. They had faded by about 80,000 years ago.

late-007.title: Lake Ouki floods the Altiplano
late-007.text: High in the Andes, a great lake once filled the Bolivian Altiplano. Lake Ouki spread there about 120,000 to 98,000 years ago, before the later Lake Tauca. Between 115,000 and 100,000 years ago its surface stood above 3,720 m. Over the same span, Lake Ballivián filled the Titicaca basin.

late-008.title: Skhul and Qafzeh: modern humans in the Levant
late-008.text: Two caves in Israel hold some of the earliest Homo sapiens outside Africa. Fossils from Qafzeh and Es-Skhul date to about 120,000 to 80,000 years ago. They mark an early dispersal near the start of the Late Pleistocene, when Neanderthals also lived in the Levant. Then the trail goes cold. No later Homo sapiens fossils are known there until Manot 1, about 54,700 years ago.

late-009.title: Giant long-horned bison evolve
late-009.text: As the Laurentide ice melted about 130,000 years ago, steppe bison spread from Alaska into central North America. There they gave rise to the giant long-horned bison, Bison latifrons. It is first known from Colorado's Snowmass site about 120,000 years ago. By 60,000 years ago it had given rise to Bison antiquus, widely considered the ancestor of the modern American bison.

late-010.title: Neanderthals hunt elephants at Neumark-Nord
late-010.text: At Neumark-Nord in Germany lie the remains of at least 57 straight-tusked elephants, about 120,000 years old. Neanderthals hunted them there regularly, perhaps every 5 to 6 years, and may have rendered fat from their bones. Systematic butchery at Lehringen, Taubach and Gröbern shows the same. Hunting these giants was widespread in Eemian Germany.

late-011.title: Denny, child of a Neanderthal and a Denisovan
late-011.text: A tiny bone from Denisova Cave in Russia belonged to a 13-year-old girl with mixed parents. Her mother was a Neanderthal and her father a Denisovan, making her a first-generation hybrid. The fragment dates to between 118,100 and 79,300 years ago. She was no one-off. About 17% of the Denisova Cave Denisovan genome comes from interbreeding with Altai Neanderthals.

late-012.title: Solo Man, the last Homo erectus
late-012.text: The last known Homo erectus lived beside the Solo River in Java, about 117,000 to 108,000 years ago. These people, called Solo Man, closed a presence on Java that had begun 1.51 to 0.93 million years ago at Sangiran. Their world was changing. By 125,000 years ago a much wetter climate had made Java an island and let tropical rainforest spread. The species probably died out as rainforest replaced the savannas it depended on. It vanished long before modern humans reached the region, roughly 55,000 to 50,000 years ago, and left no living descendants.

late-014.title: The Last Glacial Period begins
late-014.text: About 115,000 years ago the warmth ended. The Last Interglacial gave way to the Last Glacial Period, which lasted until 11,700 years ago. Average temperatures dropped markedly, and warmth-loving woodland species were pushed out of northern Europe. The cold did not arrive all at once. Temperatures fell gradually through the glacial, reaching their lowest at the {{ref:late-096}}. Each region has its own name for this ice age. It is the Würm in the Alps, the Devensian in Britain and the Weichselian in northern Europe, broadly matched by the Wisconsin in North America. With so much water locked in ice, the seas fell. Much of Sundaland, the shelf linking Southeast Asia's islands, became dry land. So did most of the Persian Gulf, for most of the glacial.

late-013.title: Dansgaard–Oeschger events: sudden glacial warmings
late-013.text: Greenland could warm about 8 °C within 40 years, in the middle of an ice age. Such Dansgaard–Oeschger events, rapid climate swings, happened 25 times during the Last Glacial Period. A rise of 5 °C over 30 to 40 years was more typical. They are best recorded in Greenland ice cores, which reach back to the end of the Eemian about 115,000 years ago. They arose when ice volume and carbon dioxide were middling, a window in which the Atlantic's overturning circulation could flip between two states. Each nudged carbon dioxide up about 5 ppm and weakened the Indonesian–Australian monsoon. A 1,470-year rhythm has been proposed, but it is debated.

late-016.title: The hand axe finally disappears
late-016.text: The hand axe, a design that had spread across continents, finally went out of use. Acheulean tools vanish from the record about then. More complex Middle Paleolithic kits, such as the Mousterian and Aterian industries, replaced them. The Mousterian had already displaced the Acheulean in Europe and the Middle East by around 125,000 years ago. In East Asia it may have lasted until about 50,000 years ago.

late-017.title: The Ata supereruption in southern Japan
late-017.text: About 100,000 years ago, a caldera eruption spread the Ata tephra over southern Japan. Most estimates date it between 100,000 and 109,000 years ago. Rated VEI 7.5, it produced over 300 km³ of tephra.

late-018.title: Blombos Cave and the earliest drawing
late-018.text: A cross-hatched line on a piece of ochre may be the earliest known drawing. It comes from Blombos Cave, on South Africa's southern Cape coast. People used the cave on and off in the Middle Stone Age, about 100,000 to 70,000 years ago. They left engraved ochre, beads of marine shell and finely made bone tools. Then wind-blown sand sealed the cave about 70,000 to 68,000 years ago. People did not return until about 2,000 years ago.

late-019.title: Woolly mammoths cross into North America
late-019.text: Woolly mammoths entered North America about 100,000 years ago by crossing the Bering Strait. Where their range met that of Columbian mammoths, the two interbred. Two Late Pleistocene molars from British Columbia carry 21.6% and 34.6% Columbian ancestry. Isotopes in their remains show that Siberia stayed more uniformly cold and dry than the American side of the Bering land bridge.

late-020.title: Los Chocoyos, Central America's greatest eruption
late-020.text: Lake Atitlán in Guatemala fills the crater of the largest known eruption in Central America. The Atitlán caldera blew out about 1,220 km³ of rhyolitic ash, or 730 km³ as dense rock. Pyroclastic currents left deposits 6 to 10 m thick in Chiapas, over 130 km from the vent. The date is uncertain, between 98,000 and 75,000 years ago. The younger estimate puts it close to the Toba supereruption. Whether it disrupted the climate is disputed.

late-021.title: The last terror birds die out
late-021.text: Terror birds, flightless predators of South America, made their last stand with a small species. Psilopterus appears to have survived there until about 96,000 years ago.

late-022.title: Kikai's eruption spreads ash across Japan
late-022.text: About 94,500 years ago, the Kikai caldera in Japan erupted at VEI 7. It spread a layer of rhyolitic ash, the K-Tz tephra, from southern Kyushu to eastern Honshu and out over the Pacific, possibly as far as the Shandong Peninsula. Layered sediments in Lake Suigetsu date it to 94,500 ± 4,800 years ago.

late-023.title: Aso-4, the largest of Aso's eruptions
late-023.text: About 90,000 years ago, Aso caldera on Kyushu erupted 384 km³ of magma, measured as solid rock. That makes it at least VEI 7. Another account rates it VEI 8, spewing about a trillion cubic meters of ash.

late-025.title: Bone harpoons at Katanda
late-025.text: About 90,000 years ago, people in the Semliki River valley of Central Africa carved harpoons from bone. The Katanda harpoons date to the Middle Stone Age. Harpoons were first invented about then, in the late Middle Paleolithic. They brought fish into human diets, a hedge against starvation.

late-026.title: A glacial lake floods western Siberia
late-026.text: When ice blocked the Arctic mouths of the Ob and Yenisei, their water had nowhere to go. A vast lake pooled at the edge of the Barents-Kara Ice Sheet. Its phase 90,000 to 80,000 years ago covered about 610,000 km² and held about 15,000 km³ of water. A second phase, 60,000 to 50,000 years ago, was larger still: about 881,000 km² and 32,000 km³.

late-024.title: The Barents–Kara Ice Sheet dams Arctic rivers
late-024.text: During the Weichselian glaciation, an ice sheet buried the Barents and Kara seas and the islands of Novaya Zemlya. The Barents–Kara Ice Sheet probably reached Svalbard and Franz Josef Land as well. On land it stretched from the North Russian Plain to the North Siberian Lowland. Its ice dammed great lakes 90,000 to 80,000 and 60,000 to 50,000 years ago. These rerouted rivers that now flow north, such as the Yenisei, Ob, Pechora and Mezen.

late-027.title: Shell necklaces at Taforalt
late-027.text: Someone strung pierced sea shells into a necklace in a cave 40 km from the sea. The shells, from an 85,000 to 82,000-year-old layer at Taforalt in Morocco, are early North African evidence of modern behavior. They probably arrived through an exchange network. Working them into ornaments suggests the shells carried meaning. Marine shells served as beads in North Africa, the Near East and sub-Saharan Africa at least 30,000 years before Europe.

late-028.title: Early modern humans in southern China
late-028.text: Modern human teeth found in China are claimed to be at least 80,000 years old. Liujiang man, among the earliest modern humans in East Asia, is most often dated to at least 67,000 years ago. Finds at Zhirendong cave, possibly over 100,000 years old, may belong to the same early wave.

late-029.title: West Antarctic ice grows to the shelf edge
late-029.text: In the Eemian, about 130,000 years ago, the West Antarctic Ice Sheet had shrunk to a few small, isolated ice caps. By about 80,000 years ago it was roughly its present size. Then it grew much larger. During the Last Glacial Maximum, which this source puts about 30,000 years ago, it reached the edges of Antarctica's continental shelves.

late-030.title: Heinrich events: armadas of icebergs
late-030.text: Every so often, great fleets of icebergs broke from the Laurentide ice sheet and drifted through Hudson Strait into the North Atlantic. These are Heinrich events, best documented for the Wisconsin glaciation, about 75,000 to 11,000 years ago. As the icebergs melted they dropped rock debris onto the seafloor, leaving layers named after them. They also poured fresh water into the ocean, likely altering its circulation. The effects reached far away. Discharges between 21,000 and 11,500 years ago coincided with droughts in the subtropics. Why the ice sheet became unstable is still debated.

late-031.title: Mastodons and giant beavers retreat from the north
late-031.text: In the warm forests of the Last Interglacial, American mastodons lived in North America's far north. About 75,000 years ago, as the Wisconsin glaciation set in, they were wiped out there. That was long before people arrived. From then on mastodons lived only south of the ice sheets. Giant beavers likewise vanished from Alaska and the Yukon after 75,000 years ago as conditions grew more hostile.

late-032.title: Toba, the great supereruption
late-032.text: About 74,000 years ago, Toba on Sumatra produced one of the largest eruptions of the Cenozoic. The VEI 8 supereruption released about 2,800 km³ of magma. It left a caldera now filled by Lake Toba and dropped about 5 cm of ash over India. The eruption itself is well dated. Its effects are not. It struck during the rapid cooling into MIS 4. Whether it sped that cooling is debated, and records from the Arabian Sea suggest it did not. The Toba catastrophe theory links the eruption to a sharp fall in human numbers, a population bottleneck. That causal link remains highly controversial. Toba was enormous but not unique. Eruptions of this size happen somewhere on Earth every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

late-033.title: MIS 4: the ice sheets advance
late-033.text: Between about 71,000 and 57,000 years ago, the world plunged into a cold stage known as MIS 4. North America's Wisconsin glaciation had begun about 75,000 years ago. In northwest Europe a very cold phase peaked around 70,000 years ago, and the Sierra Nevada's Tahoe glaciation reached its maximum perhaps about then. Glaciation became continuous on Siberia's Azas Plateau. Southern Hemisphere glaciers reached their greatest extent, as Australasia, Africa and Europe grew colder and drier.

late-034.title: The Bering land bridge rises again
late-034.text: Falling seas turned the strait between Asia and North America into dry land. Glacial sea levels last exposed the Bering land bridge about 70,000 years ago. Through the Late Pleistocene, this region, Beringia, was a mosaic of living communities joining the two continents.

late-037.title: Yellowstone's most recent lava flow
late-037.text: Yellowstone has been quieter than its reputation. After its last great caldera eruption, activity there consisted of basalt flows, rhyolite domes and minor explosive deposits. Its last known magmatic eruption, a lava flow, came about 70,000 years ago.
